lessons.title: Lists, indices and traversal
lessons.prepare: Python editor, paper index/value grids and the arrays chapter. Use suitable integer input.

slides.title: Lists, indices and traversal
slides.notes: Success means load a list, identify a value by index and display each index/value pair. Explain that Python lists implement these array-style tasks. Lists can change size and hold mixed types, while some arrays have a fixed size/type. Use consistent integer values in this week’s exercises.
body: Unit 1 · Week 6 · Lesson 1
Store related values and visit them by position.

slides.title: Retrieval: repeated input
slides.notes: Allow a minute without notes, then compare. range(3) gives 0,1,2 and three passes. A running total combines inputs but does not retain each original value. Ask why storing all readings might help later. This leads to a list without suggesting lists and fixed-size arrays are identical.
body: List the values in range(3).
What does a running total retain?
How could keeping every original input help?
Compare your explanation with a partner.

slides.title: A position differs from its value
slides.notes: Model scores=[12,7,19]. The first non-negative index is 0, scores[1] is 7 and len(scores) is 3. Ask for index of value 19:2. The last valid non-negative index is len(scores)-1. Python also supports negative indexing, which is outside this introductory convention. One-dimensional access uses one index.

slides.title: Loading values with append
slides.notes: Trace suitable integer inputs 12,7,19. The empty list grows to [12], then [12,7], then [12,7,19]. append adds at the end. Initialising scores=[] happens once before repetition. int converts input text. Ask learners to mark repeated instructions and predict len(scores) after each pass:1,2,3.
body: Trace inputs 12, 7 and 19.
Which instruction retains each new value?
slides.code:
scores = []
for index in range(3):
    score = int(input("Score: "))
    scores.append(score)
print(scores)

slides.title: Traversal with each index
slides.notes: Expected output pairs 0 12,1 7,2 19. range(len(scores)) produces 0,1,2, so every stored element is visited once. Learners identify which expression is an index and which accesses a value. Support: provide a three-column trace. Stretch: explain why range(len(scores)+1) would attempt an invalid final index.
body: Predict each index/value pair.
Explain why len(scores) is the stop value.

slides.title: Your loading and display program
slides.notes: Pairs load four integers then print each index/value pair. Use 8,3,6,10: indices 0..3 and matching values. Driver types loading, navigator checks a trace, then swap for display. Every learner records predictions. Support: supply an empty list and loop headers. Stretch: replace a source value and explain why its index stays the same. Keep suitable input assumption explicit.
body: Load four integers using append.
Display every index and its stored value.
Predict first for inputs 8, 3, 6 and 10.
Swap roles and check that all four values appear once.

slides.title: Where is the last valid index?
slides.notes: For [12,7,19], correct B is 2. A is last value 19, C is length 3. scores[3] raises IndexError. Collect simultaneous choices before discussion. If several choose C, label positions on paper and recheck a two-element list. Do not imply all out-of-range Python indices are positive.
body: Its last valid non-negative index is:
Choose alone and explain index versus value.

slides.title: Exit ticket: access and explain
slides.notes: For values=[8,3,6], values[1]=3, length 3 and last valid non-negative index 2. Access uses square brackets; append adds one value. Collect individual answers to identify indexing or length support for accumulator traversal next lesson.
body: For values = [8, 3, 6], find values[1].
State the length and last non-negative index.
Explain what append does when loading input.
Describe how a traversal visits every value.

lessons.title: Totals with list traversal
lessons.prepare: Python editor, paper accumulator traces and suitable integer lists.

slides.title: Totals with list traversal
slides.notes: Success means initialise an accumulator, add every list value once and test empty, negative and ordinary cases. Link to Week 4 running totals, now processing retained values.
body: Unit 1 · Week 6 · Lesson 2
Accumulate a total by visiting every stored value.

slides.title: Retrieval: index or value?
slides.notes: For values=[4,-2,6], values[1]=-2, len 3 and non-negative indices 0,1,2. Ask learners to retrieve individually then compare. Revisit position versus value before a loop adds values rather than indices.
body: values = [4, -2, 6]
Find values[1] and len(values).
List its non-negative indices.
Compare your answers with a partner.

slides.title: A running total through the values
slides.notes: Trace total 0, then 4, then 2, then 8. for value in values supplies each stored value, not each index. += in the chapter is shorthand for total=total+value; use expanded form here. Final print outside loop runs once. Ask learners to explain why total starts before traversal.
body: Predict total after each pass.
Which name receives a stored value?
slides.code:
values = [4, -2, 6]
total = 0
for value in values:
    total = total + value
print(total)

slides.title: The accumulator trace
slides.notes: Model first row 0+4=4, learners complete total before/after:4 and 2 for -2, then 2 and 8 for 6. Pair explanations should identify negative addition reducing the running total. Support: give one completed row. Stretch: write an indexed traversal yielding the same total and explain why adding index would give a different result.

slides.title: An empty traversal still has a total
slides.notes: With values=[], body runs zero times and initial total 0 prints. With[-8,-3], total becomes-8 then-11. With[5], one pass gives 5. Learners predict before running. This total algorithm safely handles an empty list because it does not read values[0]. Distinguish this from finding an empty list’s maximum next lesson.
body: Keep the same total algorithm.
Predict for [], [-8, -3] and [5].
Run each case and compare.
Explain why an empty list needs no index access here.

slides.title: Repairing a reset inside the loop
slides.notes: This deliberately faulty code outputs 6 rather than intended 8 for[4,-2,6]. Each pass resets total, discarding previous values. Move total=0 before the loop. Swap roles and test[],[5],[-8,-3],[4,-2,6], expecting 0,5,-11,8. Faulty version with empty list would have no total binding in a fresh run; repair before testing it. Support: mark indentation. Stretch: explain why[0,0] alone hides the reset fault.
body: Predict this version’s output.
Repair it and test empty, single and negative cases.
slides.code:
values = [4, -2, 6]
for value in values:
    total = 0
    total = total + value
print(total)

slides.title: Does the loop add values or indices?
slides.notes: For values=[10,20,30], summing indices 0+1+2 gives 3. Correct B. The required value total is 60. Collect simultaneous responses; if several choose A, place index and value columns side by side. range(len(values)) supplies indices, so an indexed accumulator must add values[index].
body: A loop adds index for index in range(len(values)).
Its total is A: 60     B: 3
Choose and explain how to total the stored values.

slides.title: Exit ticket: totals and evidence
slides.notes: For[3,-1,2], running totals 3,2,4. Empty list total 0. Initialising before loop preserves earlier values. An unequal nonzero list exposes a reset error better than all zeros. Collect a trace and one justified test; use errors for a short accumulator refresher next lesson.
body: Trace the total for [3, -1, 2].
State the expected total for an empty list.
Explain where initialisation belongs.
Choose a test that exposes a reset inside the loop.

lessons.title: Minimum and maximum positions
lessons.prepare: Python editor and index/value/best-index trace grids. Establish non-empty input before inspecting index0.

slides.title: Minimum and maximum positions
slides.notes: Success means retain the position of a best value, explain first-occurrence ties and state empty-list assumptions. Use non-empty integer lists for the main algorithm, then explicitly discuss the empty case.
body: Unit 1 · Week 6 · Lesson 3
Keep a best value’s index while traversing a list.

slides.title: Retrieval: location and value
slides.notes: For values=[4,9,9], maximum value 9 appears at indices 1 and 2. Ask learners for both, then why saying 9 does not locate an occurrence. Retrieve zero-based indexing and length before deciding a tie rule.
body: values = [4, 9, 9]
What is the maximum value?
At which indices does it occur?
Explain why a value alone does not identify its position.

slides.title: The first maximum index
slides.notes: This example assumes non-empty values. Start best_index 0, comparing actual values via indexing. At index 1,9>4 updates best_index 1; at index 2,9>9 is False so retain 1. Output 1 9. State first-occurrence tie rule. best_index 0 means a valid position, not a guessed maximum value of zero.
body: Assume the list is non-empty.
Trace which index the algorithm retains.

slides.title: A trace of the best position
slides.notes: Model initial best_index 0/value 4. For index 1 compare 9>4 True and update 1; index 2 compare 9>9 False and retain 1. Learners complete rows independently before pair checking. For a fresh[8,2,7], best_index stays 0. Support: write both compared values. Stretch: explain why a one-element list makes no loop-body passes but still has maximum index 0.

slides.title: Negative values and ties
slides.notes: For[-8,-3], first maximum index 1/value-3. A guessed maximum value 0 is wrong because 0 is not present; best_index 0 correctly refers to real value-8. For[4,9,9], > retains first index 1 while >= updates to last index 2. Ask learners to commit predictions then explain the equality check. Support: label index/value separately.
body: Predict the first maximum position in [-8, -3].
Why could a guessed maximum value of 0 fail?
For [4, 9, 9], compare using > and using >=.
Which comparison keeps the first occurrence?

slides.title: Adapting the search for a minimum
slides.notes: Change > to < and keep non-empty assumption. For[-2,4,-5,-5], first minimum index 2/value-5. For[7], index 0/value 7. Learners code and trace independently then compare evidence in pairs. Strict < preserves first equal minimum, <= gives last. Support: supply header and index loop. Stretch: implement max_index as a Week 5 function returning an index for non-empty input.
body: Adapt the algorithm to find the first minimum.
Predict for [-2, 4, -5, -5] and [7].
Implement and compare expected with actual.
Explain your tie rule.

slides.title: What about an empty list?
slides.notes: Correct B: no maximum position exists. Accessing values[0] on[] raises IndexError. Check len(values)==0 first, reporting no maximum, and use the algorithm only in the non-empty branch. If several choose A, ask what element index 0 would refer to. A total of 0 for an empty list does not imply maximum index 0.
body: values = []
What is its maximum position?
A: 0     B: no maximum position exists
Choose alone. What must happen before reading values[0]?

slides.title: Exit ticket: index, value and tie rule
slides.notes: For[-4,-1,-1], first maximum index 1/value-1; >= would retain 2. First minimum is index 0/value-4. Empty list needs a guard before accessing index 0. Collect individual explanations to identify tie-rule, sign or index confusion before the temperature task.
body: Find the first maximum in [-4, -1, -1].
Give both its index and value.
Which comparison keeps the first maximum?
State the empty-list check needed before index 0.

lessons.title: The temperature list task
lessons.prepare: Python editor and blank test log. Load exactly four suitable integer temperatures per run.

slides.title: The temperature list task
slides.notes: Success means load four temperatures, display indices/values, find first minimum without min and defend test coverage. This is formative chapter transfer practice. Exact four-input contract guarantees non-empty data before the minimum search.
body: Unit 1 · Week 6 · Lesson 4
Load temperatures and find the first minimum position.

slides.title: Retrieval: a first occurrence
slides.notes: For[-2,4,-5,-5], minimum value-5 at indices 2 and 3, first index 2. Strict < keeps the earlier equal value. Ask learners to retrieve individually then compare. Revisit position versus value if they answer only-5.
body: For [-2, 4, -5, -5], identify the minimum.
Give its first index and the other equal index.
Which comparison preserves the first minimum?
Compare your explanation with a partner.

slides.title: Loading and displaying four readings
slides.notes: Trace input-2,4,-5,-5 into the list. The four accepted integer inputs guarantee length 4 and indices 0..3. Display is a separate traversal after loading. print pairs 0 -2,1 4,2 -5,3 -5. Input validation is outside this core task. Ask learners to mark the two distinct loops.
body: Predict the four index/value pairs.
Why do loading and display use separate traversals?

slides.title: Tests before the minimum search
slides.notes: Expected first minimum indices/values: [-2,4,-5,-5] ->2/-5; [6,3,8,9] ->1/3; [2,2,2,2] ->0/2. Learners predict from requirements before running. Last tied minimum would be 3 in first case, so this catches <=. Support: label indices on paper. Stretch: choose a four-value case whose minimum occurs last, e.g.[3,2,1,0] ->3/0.

slides.title: Finding the first minimum
slides.notes: This fragment follows the four-input loading code. Start lowest_index 0 at a real element. Strict < changes only for a smaller temperature. For main test, trace best indices 0,0,2,2. Final output 2 -5. If reusing this algorithm for a variable-length list, check empty input before index 0. Support: retain index/value trace columns.
body: Use this after loading four temperatures.
Trace the repeated minimum before running.

slides.title: Your program and test record
slides.notes: Learners combine loading, display and minimum search without using min. Run all predicted four-reading cases and preserve expected results. Partner challenges a tie-rule or index explanation after individual coding. Support: provide a blank loop skeleton. Stretch: separately test a reusable search with a one-element list and an empty-list guard, distinguishing those from the exactly-four-input interface.
body: Combine loading, display and first-minimum search.
Run each predicted test set without using min.
Record any fault, correction and rerun.
Ask a partner to challenge one index or tie-rule decision.

slides.title: Index 2 or the third reading?
slides.notes: Correct B: index 2 is the third reading for Python zero-based indexing. In[-2,4,-5,-5], first minimum is index 2/value-5. Displaying human position lowest_index+1 is fine, but keep zero-based index internally for access. If several choose A, label indices 0..3 above item numbers 1..4.
body: The first minimum has Python index 2.
It is A: the second reading     B: the third reading
Choose alone and explain.
How could you display a human-friendly reading number?

slides.title: Exit ticket: defend the evidence
slides.notes: For[3,1,1,4], first minimum index 1/value 1. Strict < keeps it, while <= returns 2. Equal values test the tie rule and negative values expose an unsafe guessed best value 0. Fixed four inputs ensure non-empty data; reusable search needs a guard. Collect an individual explanation before Week 7 files and reliable input.
body: For [3, 1, 1, 4], give first minimum index and value.
Explain which comparison your program uses.
Name a test that checks repeated equal values.
Why is the four-input list safe to inspect at index 0?
